learn.intro: How did Nazi Germany organise its economy and control its people at war, how did the war become a racial war of genocide, and why did Germany lose? Questions here often ask you to weigh one reason — bombing, Speer, Hitler's mistakes — against others.

sections.title: 1. Managing the war economy

blocks.p: Germany went to war short of oil, rubber and many metals, short of labour once millions were conscripted, and short of motor transport — the army that invaded the USSR in 1941 still relied heavily on horses. Production in 1939–41 was hampered by competing agencies, over-engineered weapons and the armed services' demands for custom designs.

Fritz Todt became Minister of Armaments in 1940. After his death in a plane crash in February 1942, Albert Speer took over. Speer centralised planning, standardised designs, let industrialists run production committees and used mass-production methods; armaments output roughly tripled between early 1942 and mid-1944, despite bombing.

Göring, as head of the Four-Year Plan and the Luftwaffe, lost influence through failures and inefficiency. Labour shortages were met above all with foreign workers and prisoners — about 7 million by 1944, many forced labourers treated brutally — rather than by fully mobilising German women, whom the regime was reluctant to conscript.

German technological ingenuity was real — jet aircraft, the V-1 and V-2 rockets, synthetic fuel — but it often came too late, in too small numbers, or diverted scarce resources from weapons that could be mass-produced.

evidence: Todt Armaments Minister 1940–February 1942; Speer from February 1942.
Armaments output roughly tripled between 1942 and mid-1944.
About 7 million foreign workers and prisoners by 1944.

blocks.p: Rationing began in August 1939. Living standards were cushioned in the early war years by plunder from occupied Europe, but rations were cut in 1942 and conditions worsened sharply as defeats mounted.

Allied bombing intensified from 1942. The raids on Hamburg in July 1943 killed around 40,000 people; Dresden was devastated in February 1945. Millions of homes were destroyed and many civilians evacuated. Bombing hurt morale but did not produce the collapse the Allies hoped for.

Goebbels sustained morale through radio, newsreels and films, and after Stalingrad proclaimed 'total war' in his Sportpalast speech of February 1943. Himmler, Interior Minister from August 1943, intensified repression: the People's Court handed down death sentences in rising numbers, and defeatism could be punished by death.

Opposition grew but remained small and divided: the White Rose students in Munich (the Scholls, executed in 1943); the Edelweiss Pirates, some of whom were hanged in Cologne in 1944; Bishop von Galen's 1941 sermons against the murder of disabled people; the conservative Kreisau Circle; and the army officers' July Bomb Plot (20 July 1944), led by Stauffenberg, after which thousands were arrested and around 200 executed in direct connection.

The conquest of Poland in 1939 brought about two million Jews under German rule. Himmler was made responsible for 'strengthening Germandom' — resettling ethnic Germans and expelling Poles and Jews. Jews were forced into ghettos such as Łódź and Warsaw (1940), where many died of starvation and disease.

The invasion of the USSR (June 1941) was planned as a racial war of annihilation. Einsatzgruppen — SS mobile killing units — and police battalions shot Jews, communists and others in mass executions; hundreds of thousands were murdered in the first months, and millions of Soviet prisoners of war died of hunger and neglect.

From late 1941 the regime moved to systematic murder by gas. The Wannsee Conference (20 January 1942), chaired by Heydrich, co-ordinated the 'Final Solution' across government agencies. Death camps — Chelmno, Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka and Auschwitz-Birkenau — murdered millions. About six million Jews were killed in the Holocaust, along with Roma, disabled people and others.

Historians debate whether genocide followed Hitler's long-held intention or evolved through 'cumulative radicalisation' as competing agencies, the war in the east and local initiatives escalated policy. Most now combine both: Hitler's ideology set the goal, the conditions of war shaped the timing and methods.

sections.title: 4. Losing the war

blocks.p: Balance of resources: once the USSR (June 1941) and the USA (December 1941) were at war with Germany, the Allies had far greater manpower, raw materials and industrial capacity. American and Soviet production of tanks and aircraft outstripped Germany's even at Speer's peak.

Sea power: Allied navies blockaded Germany and kept Britain supplied. The U-boat campaign was defeated in the Battle of the Atlantic by May 1943, allowing American troops and supplies to cross for the invasions of Italy and France.

Bombing: strategic bombing destroyed cities, transport and, in 1944, synthetic-oil plants. It also forced Germany to divert huge resources — fighters, anti-aircraft guns and soldiers — to air defence, a 'second front' in the air.

Hitler's strategic mistakes: invading the USSR before defeating Britain; declaring war on the USA on 11 December 1941; refusing to allow retreats, most famously at Stalingrad, where the Sixth Army surrendered in February 1943; and diverting resources to prestige projects. Hitler killed himself on 30 April 1945 and Germany surrendered on 7–8 May.

evidence: 11 December 1941: Germany declares war on the USA.
May 1943: U-boats withdrawn from the North Atlantic.
30 April 1945: Hitler's suicide; 8 May 1945: VE Day.

people.name: Heinrich Himmler
people.role: SS chief; Interior Minister from 1943; organiser of genocide.

people.name: Clemens von Galen
people.role: Bishop of Münster; preached against the murder of disabled people (1941).

vocab.def: Full mobilisation of society and economy for war.
SS mobile killing units in the east.
Nazi term for the planned murder of Europe's Jews.
Policy becoming more extreme through competition and circumstances.

misconceptions.wrong: Germany was fully mobilised for war from 1939.
misconceptions.right: Full mobilisation came only from 1942–43; early production was inefficient.

misconceptions.wrong: The Holocaust was planned in detail before the war.
misconceptions.right: Persecution escalated through stages; systematic mass murder developed in 1941–42.

misconceptions.wrong: Bombing destroyed German morale and caused collapse.
misconceptions.right: It damaged morale and diverted resources, but the regime kept control until the end.

matching.title: Match the reason for defeat to its evidence
pairs: USA and USSR outproduced Germany in tanks and aircraft
U-boats defeated in the Atlantic by May 1943
Fighters and anti-aircraft guns diverted to defend the Reich

evidence.q: Give precise evidence of Speer's impact.
evidence.model: From February 1942 Speer centralised and standardised production; armaments output roughly tripled by mid-1944 despite bombing.

evidence.q: Give precise evidence of opposition during the war.
evidence.model: White Rose leaflets (executions 1943), Galen's sermons (1941), Edelweiss Pirates hanged in Cologne (1944), the July Bomb Plot (20 July 1944).

flashcards.q: Name three shortages that hampered the German war economy.
flashcards.a: Labour, raw materials (oil, rubber, metals) and motor transport.
Central planning, standardised designs, industrialists' committees, mass production — output roughly tripled 1942–44.

flashcards.q: Why didn't the regime fully mobilise German women?
flashcards.a: Ideology (women's place in the home) and fear of damaging morale; it used foreign forced labour instead.

flashcards.q: How did Goebbels respond to Stalingrad?
flashcards.a: The 'total war' speech (February 1943) calling for full mobilisation.
Himmler became Interior Minister; more People's Court death sentences; defeatism punished by death.

flashcards.q: What role did Himmler play in genocide?
flashcards.a: Head of the SS and police, organising resettlement, the Einsatzgruppen and the death camps.

flashcards.q: Intention or radicalisation — the Holocaust debate?
flashcards.a: Intentionalists: Hitler's long-held plan. Functionalists: escalation through war, competing agencies and local initiative. Most combine both.

flashcards.q: Give two of Hitler's strategic mistakes.
flashcards.a: Invading the USSR in 1941; declaring war on the USA; 'no retreat' orders at Stalingrad.

flashcards.q: Why did sea power matter to Germany's defeat?
flashcards.a: Blockade starved Germany of resources; U-boat defeat in 1943 let US troops and supplies cross the Atlantic.
Stauffenberg's bomb failed to kill Hitler; thousands arrested, around 200 executed in direct connection.

checklist.text: I can explain the impact of shortages and the roles of Göring, Todt and Speer.
I can assess the impact of living standards and bombing, and the roles of Goebbels and Himmler.
I can judge the nature and extent of wartime opposition.
I can explain how genocide evolved, including the role of conquest in the east and of Himmler.
I can reach a judgement on the main reason for Germany's defeat.

questions.q:
Historians differ in their judgements about Nazi control of the German civilian population in the years 1939–45.
‘The Nazis were able to completely control the German civilian population in the years 1939–45.’
Assess this view using your own knowledge of the issue.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q:
Historians differ in their judgements about the reasons for Germany's defeat in the Second World War.
‘Germany was defeated in the years 1941–45 mainly because of Hitler's strategic mistakes.’
Assess this view using your own knowledge of the issue.

stretch.task: Was Speer's 'armaments miracle' a miracle at all? Consider what had been wasted before 1942 and the role of forced labour.
Was the war lost in the factories or on the battlefield? Compare the balance of resources with Hitler's mistakes using effectiveness and impact.
How can historians explain why so many ordinary Germans continued to work and fight until 1945?
